items.text: All provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

segments.text: The CPC is the main procedural framework for how civil litigation is instituted, conducted, decided and enforced.

Think of the CPC as the life-cycle of a civil case: parties and jurisdiction, institution of suit, pleadings, summons, appearance, issues, evidence, judgment and decree, execution, appeals/review/revision, and special procedures. The precise legal effect comes from the Code, Orders and Rules.
Primary authority: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (current applicable text and rules).

The CPC is the procedural architecture through which civil rights are asserted, contested, adjudicated and enforced. Substantive law may tell a person that a contractual, proprietary or other civil right exists; procedure tells the person how to bring the claim before a competent court and how the court should move from pleading to enforceable decision.

The most effective way to learn the Code is to connect each procedural rule to a stage of litigation. This prevents the common problem of memorizing isolated sections or Orders without understanding why they exist.

blocks.text: Civil suit as a process map

segments.text: A typical civil-case map begins with jurisdiction and institution of suit. It then moves to identification of parties, pleadings, service of summons, appearance and preliminary objections, admission or denial, framing of issues, discovery or production of material where applicable, evidence and hearing, judgment, decree or order, and finally execution. Alongside the main route are interim remedies, commissions, withdrawal or compromise, special procedures and post-judgment remedies.

Pleadings and issues perform different functions. Pleadings set out the material case of each side; issues identify the propositions of fact or law that genuinely require adjudication. Evidence should then be directed to those disputed propositions rather than becoming an uncontrolled narrative.

A judgment gives the court’s reasons and determination. A decree is the formal expression of an adjudication that conclusively determines rights regarding matters in controversy in the suit to the extent defined by the Code. An order is a formal decision that is not a decree. These distinctions matter because the availability of appeal, execution or other remedies can depend on the legal character of the court’s decision.

Execution is the stage at which an adjudicated right is translated into practical relief. A successful litigant may still need judicial machinery to obtain possession, recover money, enforce an injunction or otherwise secure the benefit of the decree. Procedure therefore continues after the merits have been decided.

Appeal, review and revision should be learned separately. An appeal exists because legislation confers it and ordinarily allows a higher forum to reconsider the decision within the scope of the appeal. Review is a limited reconsideration by the same court under legally defined grounds. Revision is supervisory and addresses jurisdictional or procedural error within the statutory limits of revisional power. None of these concepts should be used interchangeably.

Two additional distinctions frequently cause confusion. Res sub judice concerns the effect of an already pending suit involving the legally required identity of issues and parties; res judicata concerns the finality of a matter already adjudicated. Set-off and counterclaim both permit defensive or responsive claims in a suit, but their legal requirements and procedural operation differ.

items.text: Understand the CPC as the route map of a civil case. A civil right may exist under substantive law, but the CPC provides the machinery for bringing that right before a court and obtaining an enforceable decision.

The life-cycle is easier than section-by-section memorization: jurisdiction and institution of suit; pleadings; service and appearance; framing of issues; evidence and hearing; judgment, decree or order; execution; and available corrective remedies.
Pleadings tell the court what each side claims. Issues convert those competing claims into precise questions for trial. Evidence is then directed toward proving or disproving those questions.
Execution is a separate but essential stage. Winning a decree is not always the end; the successful party may need the court's execution machinery to obtain the practical benefit of the decree.
Keep the main corrective mechanisms separate:

an appeal is a statutory rehearing or reconsideration by a higher forum; review is reconsideration by the same court within limited grounds; revision is supervisory correction within the scope given by law.

rows: Common confusion to avoid: Do not memorize Orders and sections without understanding where they appear in the life-cycle of a suit. Sequence is the key to this paper.

Civil procedure tells the court and parties how a civil right is enforced.
Pleadings define the controversy.
Issues identify disputed questions for trial.
A decree formally determines rights in a suit; execution enforces it.
Appeal is statutory; review and revision have different purposes and limits.
